## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is that the original Vision Transformer's strongest claim cannot be converted into a data-independent backbone ranking. Dosovitskiy et al. showed that a pure transformer over image patches could perform very well after large-scale pretraining and transfer, but CvT's authors describe ViT as remaining below similarly sized CNN counterparts such as ResNets when trained on smaller datasets. Battle of the Backbones later reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. The practical implication is that comparisons must state corpus size, transfer target, model size, and whether training is supervised or self-supervised; otherwise a large-data ViT result and a small-data CNN result answer different questions. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea]

A second unresolved issue is how to compare backbones fairly when pretraining recipes differ. Battle of the Backbones found supervised convolutional networks strongest on most tasks in its broad suite, but also observed that the supervised models often benefited from larger pretraining datasets; when architecture and dataset scale were matched, self-supervised backbones were highly competitive or better. Thus, architecture family, pretraining objective, and data scale are entangled. The available evidence does not justify attributing every CNN or ViT advantage solely to convolution or self-attention, and the original ViT-versus-CNN question remains conditional unless those variables are controlled. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

Dense prediction exposes a concrete task-interface limitation of original ViT. Its columnar, coarse patch tokens produce a single-scale, low-resolution representation, while detection and segmentation commonly need high-resolution, multi-stage feature maps; PVT also notes that global attention becomes computationally and memory expensive at image sizes around an 800-pixel short edge. CNN backbones already provide progressively downsampled feature maps, but that convenience is not the same as proving better classification accuracy. The open problem is to obtain global context, dense spatial detail, and multiscale outputs without paying the full cost of long token sequences or redesigning the original ViT interface. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012]

Later systems show plausible fixes, but they also change the object being evaluated. PVT adds 4×4 patches, a progressive shrinking pyramid, and spatial-reduction attention; CvT adds convolutional token embedding, hierarchical stages, and convolutional projections; ViT-CoMer adds a convolutional multi-receptive-field pyramid and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion. These designs address hierarchy, locality, or token cost, yet their results cannot be assigned to the original pure ViT. A remaining evaluation problem is therefore to disentangle gains from the attention mechanism itself from gains introduced by CNN-style pyramids, convolutions, new tokenization, or the ability to reuse particular pretrained weights. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0]

The efficiency question is also not settled by one scalar metric. Original global self-attention mixes all patch tokens, so finer patches and higher resolutions rapidly increase sequence-related compute and memory; HVT and PVT respond by pooling or spatially reducing tokens, while LeViT adopts decreasing activation-map resolutions in a hybrid fast classifier. However, parameters, FLOPs, CPU latency, GPU latency, peak memory, and token count measure different constraints. LeViT's reported five-fold CPU speed advantage over EfficientNet at 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy is hardware- and model-specific, and it cannot be generalized into a universal transformer-versus-CNN efficiency conclusion from FLOPs alone. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:3e86efa21051]

High-resolution multimodal use intensifies the token-budget problem rather than resolving the backbone comparison. ConvLLaVA replaces ViT with a hierarchical ConvNeXt encoder because redundant visual tokens create substantial compute in high-resolution large multimodal models; after high-resolution adaptation and an added compression stage, it supports 1536×1536 inputs with 576 visual tokens. This demonstrates a strong task-specific reason to favor hierarchical convolutional compression, but it is not an ImageNet-controlled comparison with original ViT. The open problem is to compare visual encoders under the same multimodal decoder, resolution, token budget, accuracy target, and hardware budget rather than inferring universal superiority from token reduction. [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:8b6f0b7a6a17]

Representation research raises another open problem: similar task accuracy can hide different internal strategies. CKA analyses find that ViTs maintain more uniform representations across layers, whereas ResNets separate more clearly into lower and higher stages; the study links early global information aggregation to self-attention and strong lower-to-upper feature propagation to ViT residual connections. These differences may affect robustness, localization, fine-tuning, and interpretability, but CKA similarity alone does not establish which representation is preferable. More controlled work is needed to connect architectural mechanism and representation geometry to out-of-distribution behavior, spatial localization, and transfer performance. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:ea90270388d2] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:02ab8c9650c5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:52af6f3b7abb] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31]

The conceptual boundary between Transformers and ConvNets also remains open. A unified framework interprets vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions and uses that view to replace softmax with ReLU plus Layer Normalization and to design a depth-wise vision Transformer with comparable performance and greater efficiency in its experiments. Such unification helps compare kernel banks, dynamic weights, depth-wise operations, and activation choices, but it does not show that original ViT and a static CNN backbone have identical inductive biases or deployment costs. Researchers still need evidence about which shared design components cause convergence, accuracy, or efficiency changes. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:733cf6749238] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:d87b9e51465a] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:3:0c1521ca20ba:claim:683bed3275bc]

Finally, hybrid and modernized backbones complicate reproducibility for practitioners. ViT-CoMer preserves a plain ViT branch so it can load open-source ViT pretraining while newly added convolutional components use different initialization; CvT removes the need for conventional positional encoding in its convolutional design; and broad benchmarks include ConvNeXt, ResNet, SwinV2, CLIP ViT, self-supervised models, and diffusion-derived encoders. This diversity means a backbone chosen for one regime may not be best for another. The concrete limitation is not a lack of models, but the difficulty of making an informed choice without matched data, task, resolution, token budget, latency, pretraining, and downstream-head conditions. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

Overall, the evidence supports a trade-off rather than a final winner. Original ViT removes convolution and gains early global mixing and a generic sequence architecture, with its best evidence under large-scale pretraining; convolutional neural-network backbones retain local weight sharing, built-in hierarchy, and dense-feature interfaces that can help under smaller-data, efficiency, or dense-prediction constraints. Adapted and hybrid models improve specific weaknesses, but each modification narrows the claim. The central open problem is therefore not whether one family is universally better, but how to isolate and match the conditions under which global attention, convolutional locality, hierarchy, token compression, and pretraining actually determine performance. ## Conclusion

The answer to the comparison is that original ViT and convolutional neural-network backbones make different architectural trades. ViT removes convolutional locality and processes image patches as a global token sequence; this supports its strongest large-data transfer results but increases attention cost as token count grows and leaves a coarse classification-oriented representation. CNN backbones encode local weight sharing and stage-wise hierarchy, making them natural feature extractors for smaller-data learning and dense-prediction frameworks, without proving universal accuracy superiority. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636]

Experimental claims must remain matched to their conditions. The original ViT result supports viability under large-scale pretraining and transfer; CvT's small-data statement and Battle of the Backbones' finding that ViTs are more sensitive to pretraining-data amount and parameter count qualify rather than overturn it. PVT's COCO gains over ResNet50 or ResNeXt101, CvT's 87.7% ImageNet-1k result, and ViT-CoMer's COCO/ADE20K scores belong to adapted or hybrid systems, not to unmodified ViT. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:f3405d317606] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

CNN backbones are convenient when local priors, hierarchical maps, constrained pretraining or dense tasks dominate; original ViT is compelling when large corpora support learning visual structure and early global context is valuable. synthesis.draft:
# Original Vision Transformer and Convolutional Backbones: A Mechanism, Data-Scale, and Task-Fit Comparison

## Abstract

This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones using architecture and training regime as the organizing choice. Strictly, ViT is Dosovitskiy et al.'s convolution-free patch-sequence classifier: fixed patches are linearly embedded, augmented with position information, and processed by global self-attention/MLP encoder blocks. CNN backbones such as ResNet and ResNeXt instead use local, weight-shared convolution, depth-dependent receptive-field growth, and usually hierarchical feature maps. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a]

The central scientific finding is conditional rather than a universal ranking. ViT compared strongly with state-of-the-art convolutional networks and required substantially fewer training computational resources in its reported large-scale pretraining-and-transfer setting, including ImageNet, CIFAR-100 and VTAB; smaller-data training is a different regime, where cited later work says ViT remained below similarly sized CNN counterparts. Global attention also brings quadratic token complexity, and ViT's coarse, single-scale token grid is not the ready-made multi-stage interface that CNN backbones offer detection and segmentation heads. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea]

PVT, CvT, HVT, LeViT, ViT-CoMer and broad benchmarks such as Battle of the Backbones illuminate trade-offs but change the evaluated object or population: they add pyramids, pooling, convolutions, hybrid inference designs, modern pretraining or different task heads. Their results should therefore not be reassigned to original ViT. Across the cited evidence, CNNs contribute locality and built-in hierarchy, whereas original ViT supplies early global mixing with greater dependence on data scale; performance depends on task, resolution, model budget, pretraining and downstream interface. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:f3405d317606] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:3e86efa21051] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012]

## Introduction

This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones, using architecture and training regime as the organizing choice rather than treating every later hybrid or dense-prediction transformer as the same model. The central question is not simply which family has higher accuracy in one table: ViT replaced the conventional convolutional stack with a pure sequence model over image patches, whereas CNN backbones such as ResNet, ResNeXt, and later ConvNeXt build features through local, weight-shared convolution and typically hierarchical feature maps. The comparison therefore needs to keep mechanism, pretraining data, output resolution, downstream task, and compute or parameter budget together. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea]

The original Vision Transformer is specifically Dosovitskiy et al.'s convolution-free image-classification model: an image is divided into fixed patches, patches are linearly embedded, position information is added, and standard Transformer encoder layers process the resulting tokens. Its headline claim was conditional: when pretrained on large data and transferred to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks, ViT compared strongly with state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train. This does not establish that a randomly initialized or small-data ViT generally beats a CNN; later work explicitly reports that ViT under similarly sized CNN counterparts when trained on smaller data, citing CNNs' built-in local visual biases as a plausible reason. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67]

Convolutional neural-network backbones provide the reference design against which original ViT should be judged. A convolution kernel scans the image with shared weights, giving local receptive fields that grow as depth increases; ResNet's skip connections enabled very deep convolutional stacks, while multi-path designs such as ResNeXt expanded the convolutional block design space. These inductive biases suit the strong two-dimensional local structure of natural images, and CNNs were the default ImageNet-pretrained feature extractors before the rapid expansion of transformer backbones. Battle of the Backbones later found that, among the diverse pretrained models and tasks it benchmarked, supervised large-data convolutional backbones remained strongest on most tasks, although that conclusion concerns a broad modern model suite and is not a direct test of the original ViT paper's exact setup. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

The comparison also changes with the target task. Original ViT was primarily an image-recognition architecture with a columnar, coarse patch representation; dense-prediction papers identify single-scale, low-resolution outputs and high memory or attention cost as obstacles when applying that design directly to detection and segmentation. CNN backbones naturally expose hierarchical feature maps, and transformer successors such as PVT add pyramids and spatial-reduction attention to become drop-in replacements in dense-prediction frameworks. Hybrid models such as CvT and ViT-CoMer further blur the boundary by introducing convolutions or convolutional multiscale features into transformer systems, so they are evidence for design trade-offs rather than examples of the original pure ViT. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

This taxonomy uses architecture and training regime as its organizing choice: first separate the original Vision Transformer from convolutional neural-network backbones, then locate later models by how much they retain each family's token-mixing, spatial hierarchy, and convolutional bias. This is a review grouping for comparison, not a universal taxonomy and not a partition asserted by the original ViT paper. It also avoids treating accuracy, efficiency, dense-prediction suitability, and multimodal use as interchangeable labels: a model can be accurate in classification but awkward as a detection backbone, or efficient at one resolution but costly at another. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:8b6f0b7a6a17]

At the pure-CNN end, backbones compute feature maps with locally connected, weight-shared convolutions; their effective receptive field expands with depth, and common detection or segmentation frameworks consume their multi-stage pyramid of feature maps. ResNet and ResNeXt belong here, with residual and multi-path convolutional blocks respectively. The relevant comparison criteria are local spatial bias, translation-equivariant weight sharing, hierarchical resolution, and readiness for dense-prediction heads. These criteria describe the backbone family; they do not by themselves imply higher accuracy than transformers under every pretraining setting. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a]

The original Vision Transformer occupies the pure-transformer end of this grouping. It replaces the convolutional stack with non-overlapping patch embedding, positional information, a class token, and repeated global self-attention/MLP encoder blocks. Its defining criteria are sequence-wide token mixing, a columnar representation rather than a CNN-style stage pyramid, and dependence on large-scale pretraining for its strongest transfer results. Thus, “ViT” in the strict comparison means Dosovitskiy et al.'s image-classification model, not every later model with “Vision Transformer” in its name. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a]

A second axis is task interface. Original ViT was designed for image recognition and normally produces a single-scale, relatively coarse representation from patches such as 16×16 or 32×32 pixels; PVT's authors identify this low-resolution output and the high cost of attention on large feature maps as reasons why ViT is difficult to plug directly into pixel-level detection and segmentation pipelines. CNN backbones, by contrast, are conventionally organized around downsampled feature-map stages. PVT is therefore classified as a convolution-free transformer backbone adapted to dense prediction, using fine patches, a progressive shrinking pyramid, and spatial-reduction attention; it is not the original ViT architecture. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60]

Hybrid models form a third, deliberately mixed group rather than evidence that pure ViT and CNNs are identical. CvT introduces convolutional token embedding and convolutional projections inside a hierarchical transformer, while ViT-CoMer preserves a plain ViT branch that can load open-source ViT pretraining and adds a convolutional multiscale feature pyramid plus bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion. Their classification criterion is which components are changed: they import locality, overlapping or hierarchical features, and multiscale reception into a transformer system. Consequently, their results should be attributed to the hybrid design and its training, not used as direct measurements of original ViT. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842]

Efficiency-oriented variants require a separate criterion because token reduction, hierarchical pooling, hardware speed, and parameter/FLOP budgets answer different questions. HVT progressively pools visual tokens to shorten the sequence and analogizes this reduction to CNN downsampling, whereas LeViT reuses CNN principles such as decreasing activation-map resolutions in a hybrid fast-classification network. These models may improve a speed–accuracy trade-off, but FLOPs or parameters alone do not establish latency across hardware. Likewise, ConvLLaVA's use of ConvNeXt to reduce excessive visual tokens in high-resolution multimodal models is a downstream encoder-design comparison, not a classification-backbone test of original ViT against CNNs. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:3e86efa21051] [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:8b6f0b7a6a17]

Finally, representational and unification studies should be classified as analyses rather than backbone categories. CKA comparisons show that ViTs and ResNets can develop different internal representation structures: ViT representations are more uniform across layers, while ResNet representations separate more strongly by lower and higher stages. A separate unified interpretation casts vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions to compare design choices and derive alternatives such as ReLU-normalized or depth-wise variants. That conceptual relationship does not erase the architectural distinction; it means locality, global mixing, hierarchy, dynamic kernels, pretraining, and task interface must be compared separately. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:ea90270388d2] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:02ab8c9650c5] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:733cf6749238] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:d87b9e51465a]

## Representative Methods

The original Vision Transformer's core mechanism is a direct replacement of the convolutional visual pipeline by a sequence model. Dosovitskiy et al. split an image into fixed, non-overlapping patches, linearly project flattened patches into embeddings, add positional embeddings, prepend a learned class token, and apply standard Transformer encoder blocks built from multi-head self-attention and MLPs. Its contribution is therefore architectural rather than a new attention operator: the paper argues that reliance on CNNs is unnecessary and that a pure transformer applied directly to image patches can perform very well on image classification after large-scale pretraining and transfer. The applicability boundary is important: this claim is about the original patch-based ViT under its pretraining-and-transfer protocol, not about every later hierarchical, convolutional, distilled, or dense-prediction model using the ViT name. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67]

Self-attention gives original ViT a different spatial-computation pattern from a conventional CNN. In one attention layer, tokens can exchange information across the entire image rather than only within a local convolution window; positional embeddings supply spatial order because patch tokens and attention weights do not otherwise encode absolute patch locations. This creates global context early in the network, which representation analyses identify as a major difference from ResNet-like models whose local receptive fields are initially small and expand through depth. The trade-off is that global mixing over a full patch sequence has quadratic token complexity, so fine patches or high-resolution images increase attention compute and memory rapidly. That mechanism explains why original ViT is especially effective when enough data supports learning visual relations without convolution's built-in locality, but it also motivates later token pooling, spatial reduction, windowing, and hybrid convolution designs. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31]

The original ViT's columnar token representation should be distinguished from the hierarchical feature maps expected by many dense-prediction systems. It keeps one token grid at the patch resolution through repeated encoder blocks and typically uses the class token or global feature for classification; with common patch sizes such as 16×16 or 32×32 pixels, the spatial output is coarse relative to detection and segmentation feature needs. PVT's authors explicitly identify two obstacles in adapting that design directly to pixel-level tasks: ViT produces a single-scale, low-resolution feature map, and its compute and memory costs become high at the larger image sizes common in COCO-style detection. Thus, original ViT is best understood first as an image-recognition architecture that can be transferred, not as a ready-made multi-stage replacement for ResNet in RetinaNet or Mask R-CNN. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60]

Convolutional neural-network backbones use a contrasting mechanism. A convolution kernel is applied across spatial locations with shared weights, creating local connectivity and translation-equivariant feature extraction; neighboring pixels are combined within the kernel, and repeated layers enlarge the effective receptive field as depth increases. PVT's review of CNN backbones describes this local-kernel structure and notes that ResNet introduced skip connections that made very deep convolutional networks practical, while multi-path blocks such as those in ResNeXt broadened convolutional block designs. These networks usually progressively downsample activation maps and expose stages at different strides and semantic levels. That hierarchy is a useful interface for detection and segmentation heads, but it is an architectural property of CNN backbones, not proof of superior classification accuracy under all training regimes. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a]

The CNN contribution in this comparison is therefore a strong set of learned and built-in visual priors: locality, weight sharing, spatial hierarchy, and depth-based receptive-field growth. CvT's authors summarize the small-data side of the contrast by noting that, despite vision Transformers' large-scale success, ViT remained below similarly sized CNN counterparts such as ResNets when trained on smaller datasets; they suggest that CNNs inherently encode properties suited to images, whose nearby pixels are strongly correlated. This does not mean CNNs always generalize better. It means that convolutional structure reduces some of what the model must learn from data, whereas the original ViT's more generic sequence-processing architecture benefits substantially from large pretraining corpora. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012]

The data-scale condition is central to interpreting ViT's evidence. The original paper's strongest statement is conditional: when pretrained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small recognition benchmarks, including ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and VTAB, ViT attained excellent results compared with state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train. Battle of the Backbones later reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and number of parameters, and that supervised convolutional networks were strongest on most tasks in its broad modern benchmark. These findings are complementary rather than directly rankable: the latter evaluates a diverse suite of backbones, tasks, and modern pretraining methods, whereas the original ViT claim concerns specific models, datasets, transfer settings, and training-compute comparisons. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea]

Representation analyses further show that the two backbone mechanisms do not merely produce the same features with different operators. CKA comparisons between ViTs and ResNets find that ViTs have a much more uniform layer-similarity structure, with lower and higher ViT layers more similar to one another, whereas ResNet representations divide more clearly into lower and higher stages. Cross-model CKA indicated that many lower ResNet layers were needed to resemble representations near the lower part of ViT, while the final portion of ViT was less aligned with the ResNet stages examined. The same analysis attributes an important role to self-attention in early global-information aggregation and to ViT residual connections in strongly propagating lower-layer features upward. These are mechanistic observations about learned representations, not evidence that one family is universally more accurate. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:ea90270388d2] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:02ab8c9650c5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:52af6f3b7abb] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31]

The original ViT's residual path also changes how information persists through depth. In the CKA study, ViT residual connections were found to strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers, helping explain the relatively uniform representation structure across transformer layers. ResNets likewise use residual connections to train very deep convolutional stacks, but their stage-wise changes in resolution and channels produce stronger representational separation across groups of layers. Consequently, both families can benefit from skip connections, yet the surrounding computation differs: ViT repeats globally mixing transformer blocks on a common token sequence, while CNN backbones stack local convolutional blocks across changing spatial resolutions. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:ea90270388d2] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012]

PVT illustrates how later transformer backbones borrow the task-fit properties of CNNs without becoming the original ViT. It starts from fine-grained 4×4 patches to obtain high-resolution features, progressively shrinks the sequence in a pyramid analogous to CNN stage downsampling, and uses spatial-reduction attention to control the cost of high-resolution features. The authors state that, unlike traditional CNN backbones whose local receptive fields grow with depth, PVT maintains a global receptive field and is therefore aimed at detection and segmentation; unlike original ViT, its pyramid can be inserted into dense-prediction pipelines such as RetinaNet and Mask R-CNN. PVT should thus be treated as an adapted convolution-free transformer backbone, not as evidence that the original ViT already provided the same multi-scale interface. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd]

CvT represents a different response to the ViT–CNN comparison: it deliberately imports convolutional mechanisms into a transformer. It uses convolutional token embedding in a hierarchy of transformer stages and convolutional projections in transformer blocks. The stated design goal is to add CNN-like properties—shift, scale, and distortion invariance as characterized by the paper—while retaining transformer properties such as dynamic attention, global context, and better generalization. CvT also reports that positional encoding can be removed in that design, simplifying higher-resolution use. Its mechanism and evidence belong to a hybrid model, so CvT's ImageNet or transfer results cannot be assigned to the original pure ViT; they show that convolutional tokenization and projection can alter ViT's efficiency and inductive bias. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67]

ViT-CoMer is another hybrid, but it addresses dense-prediction limitations while preserving a plain ViT branch. It adds a spatial-pyramid, multi-receptive-field convolutional feature path and a CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion module so that convolutional local and multiscale features interact with transformer features. The authors target two deficiencies they attribute to plain ViT in dense prediction: lack of inner-patch local interaction and limited feature-scale diversity. Because the ViT module can directly use open-source pretrained ViT weights while added components are initialized differently, ViT-CoMer is a feature-enhanced backbone rather than a modification that proves the original architecture was already multiscale. Its reported COCO and ADE20K results are examined as downstream-task evidence, not as a pure architecture-versus-CNN classification result. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:f3405d317606]

Hierarchical Visual Transformer addresses token redundancy rather than convolution itself. HVT progressively pools visual tokens, shortening the sequence in a way the authors analogize to feature-map downsampling in CNNs; this allows depth, width, resolution, or patch size to scale with less additional computational complexity. The paper also reports empirically that average-pooled visual tokens contain more discriminative information than a single class token in its setting. HVT is useful for understanding that original ViT's fixed full-length sequence and class-token classifier are design choices, not necessary features of all vision transformers. Its comparable-FLOP ImageNet and CIFAR-100 comparisons concern an efficiency-modified architecture and should not be read as measurements of unmodified ViT. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b]

LeViT makes the efficiency boundary even clearer by being explicitly hybrid. It re-applies convolutional-network principles—especially activation maps with decreasing resolutions—to transformer-style fast inference and introduces attention bias for positional information. Its target is the speed–accuracy trade-off in image classification across hardware measures, with the paper reporting, for example, that at 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy LeViT is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. This is evidence that hierarchy, downsampling, and hybrid design can improve inference efficiency, but it is not a like-for-like comparison between original ViT and a standard CNN backbone. Hardware-specific speed also cannot be inferred from parameters or FLOPs alone. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:3e86efa21051]

A unification perspective argues that vision Transformers can be interpreted as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions, placing existing transformers and dynamic ConvNets in one design framework. Under that interpretation, self-attention resembles spatially dynamic kernel construction rather than a wholly unrelated operation; the framework supports side-by-side comparisons of design choices such as softmax activation, global kernel banks, and depth-wise operations. The same paper reports two design studies: replacing softmax with ConvNet-style ReLU and Layer Normalization yielded faster convergence and better performance in its experiments, and a depth-wise vision Transformer was more efficient with comparable performance. This conceptual bridge does not eliminate the practical distinction between original ViT and static CNN backbones; it shows that some mechanisms can be analyzed as points in a shared dynamic-convolution design space. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:733cf6749238] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:d87b9e51465a] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:3:0c1521ca20ba:claim:683bed3275bc]

Modern convolutional backbones also complicate any simple “old CNN versus ViT” story. ConvNeXt is a hierarchical convolutional encoder that can serve as a visual backbone outside classification; ConvLLaVA uses ConvNeXt instead of ViT in a high-resolution large multimodal model because hierarchical convolutional compression reduces excessive visual tokens. After adapting ConvNeXt to high resolution and adding a successive compression stage, ConvLLaVA supports 1536×1536 inputs with 576 visual tokens and arbitrary aspect ratios while reporting competitive multimodal-benchmark performance. This is a task-specific encoder comparison at very high resolution, not evidence that ConvNeXt generally outperforms original ViT on ImageNet. It does, however, reinforce the importance of hierarchy and token compression when global ViT attention would face many visual tokens. [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:8b6f0b7a6a17]

The broad benchmark evidence should be separated from architectural mechanism. Battle of the Backbones compares many pretrained feature extractors across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization, and other tasks using over 1,500 training runs. Its summary names supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-supervised SwinV2-Base, and CLIP ViT-Base as top models overall, with ConvNeXt-Tiny and SwinV2-Tiny strong at smaller scales, and states that supervised convolutional networks outperform transformers on most considered tasks. It also qualifies the pretraining conclusion: when architecture and pretraining-dataset size are matched apples-to-apples, self-supervised backbones are highly competitive or better. Because this suite includes modern hierarchical transformers, CLIP, self-supervised models, ConvNeXt, and ResNet, it does not directly reproduce the original ViT-versus-CNN experiment. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

The applicability boundary for CNN backbones is therefore not universality either. Their local priors and pyramidal stages make them natural, well-established feature extractors and often strong choices when pretraining data, model size, or dense-prediction interfaces are constrained. Yet convolutional locality can also delay global integration until deeper layers, and modern benchmark winners include hierarchical transformers, language-image pretrained ViTs, and convolutional models trained on large datasets. The supported conclusion is comparative: original ViT trades convolutional locality and a built-in multi-stage map for early global token mixing and a generic transformer architecture, while CNN backbones exploit local weight sharing and hierarchy; which choice gives better performance depends on data scale, model scale, resolution, task head, and evaluation budget. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea]

Accordingly, the methods comparison should preserve three levels of claims. At the architecture level, original ViT is pure patch-sequence self-attention without convolution, whereas CNN backbones are local, weight-shared, hierarchical feature extractors. At the learning level, ViT's strongest original evidence depends on large-scale pretraining and transfer, while CNN inductive biases can be advantageous with smaller data. At the task-interface level, original ViT is naturally a recognition model with coarse single-scale tokens, whereas CNN stages and adapted transformer variants such as PVT, CvT, HVT, and ViT-CoMer add hierarchy, convolution, pooling, or multiscale fusion for efficiency and dense prediction. Later hybrids and benchmarks inform the trade-off, but they do not collapse the distinction between the original Vision Transformer and convolutional neural-network backbones. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison should be read around matched conditions rather than as one universal ranking. The original Vision Transformer paper reports a conditional large-scale transfer result: after pretraining on large data, ViT attained excellent results on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks relative to state-of-the-art convolutional networks, while using substantially fewer computational resources to train. That comparison supports pure patch-sequence transformers as viable CNN replacements under the paper's large-data regime; it does not show that an otherwise matched ViT wins when pretraining data are small. CvT's authors explicitly state the complementary small-data limitation: ViT performance remained below similarly sized CNN counterparts such as ResNets when trained on smaller amounts of data. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] The closest architectural contrast in the evidence is therefore data-conditioned. CNN backbones such as ResNet and ResNeXt enter the comparison with local convolution, shared kernels, stage-wise downsampling and established ImageNet representations, which reduces the amount of visual structure that must be learned from scratch. Original ViT instead relies on non-overlapping patch embeddings, positional information and global self-attention; its strongest recognition results appear when large pretraining corpora allow that generic sequence model to learn visual regularities. Because the cited ViT claim compares against state-of-the-art convolutional networks under specific large-scale transfer protocols, while CvT discusses the small-data regime rather than supplying the same full benchmark table here, the two findings should not be merged into a single head-to-head score. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012]

Representation experiments provide a separate dimension from top-1 accuracy. CKA analyses of ViTs and ResNets compare layer-pair representations and find that ViTs have a much more uniform similarity structure, including greater similarity between lower and higher layers, whereas ResNet representations separate more clearly into lower and higher stages. In cross-model CKA comparisons, the lower half of a 60-layer ResNet was similar to roughly the lowest quarter of ViT layers, the top half of ResNet was approximately similar to the next third of ViT layers, and the final third of ViT was less aligned with the examined ResNet stages. These measurements explain how the models differ internally—early global attention and strong residual propagation in ViT versus stage-wise convolutional feature transformation—but they do not by themselves rank predictive accuracy. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:ea90270388d2] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:02ab8c9650c5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:52af6f3b7abb] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31]

Dense-prediction experiments expose a task-interface mismatch between original ViT and conventional CNN backbones. PVT's authors argue that ViT is difficult to apply directly to detection and segmentation because its columnar coarse-patch output is single-scale and low-resolution, while global attention on high-resolution images is computationally and memory expensive. In the reported RetinaNet comparison on COCO val2017, under a comparable parameter count, PVT-Small achieved 40.4 AP versus 36.3 AP for ResNet50, a difference of 4.1 absolute AP points; PVT-Large achieved 42.6 AP, 1.6 points above ResNeXt101-64x4d while using 30% fewer parameters. These are PVT results from an adapted pyramid transformer with fine patches and spatial-reduction attention, not results for the original ViT, so they cannot be interpreted as original ViT beating CNN backbones. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] The PVT experiment is nevertheless informative about why CNN-like hierarchy matters in dense frameworks. Traditional CNN backbones produce multi-stage feature maps that detectors and segmenters already consume, while original ViT produces a coarse token grid aimed primarily at classification. PVT changes the interface by using 4×4 patches, progressively shrinking the token sequence and applying spatial-reduction attention; it also claims a global receptive field throughout rather than the depth-dependent local receptive-field growth of CNNs. Thus, the supported comparison is three-way: CNNs offer a ready-made hierarchical map, original ViT offers global mixing but a poor unmodified dense-prediction interface, and PVT is a convolution-free redesign intended to combine global attention with a CNN-like pyramid. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012]

Hybrid experiments show that adding convolutional structure can improve ViT-oriented models, but they are not tests of the original pure architecture. CvT replaces ViT's non-overlapping linear patch embedding with convolutional token embedding in a hierarchy and uses convolutional projections in transformer blocks; on ImageNet-1k it reports state-of-the-art performance relative to other Vision Transformers and ResNets with fewer parameters and lower FLOPs in its comparisons, and an ImageNet-22k-pretrained CvT-W24 reaches 87.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k validation. Those numbers belong to CvT's hierarchical convolutional-transformer design and its training setting. They support the value of locality and hierarchy as design modifications, not a claim that Dosovitskiy et al.'s original ViT attained that result. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] ViT-CoMer supplies dense-prediction evidence for a different hybrid construction. It retains a plain ViT branch that can load open-source ViT pretrained weights, while adding a convolutional multi-receptive-field pyramid and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion to address limited inner-patch interaction and single-scale features. The reported ViT-CoMer-L result is 64.3% AP on COCO val2017 without extra detection training data such as Objects365, together with 62.1% mIoU on ADE20K validation. The paper describes the ADE20K score as comparable to state-of-the-art methods and notes that advanced open-source pretraining such as DINOv2 improves performance. Because the evaluated system includes convolutional feature enhancement and task-specific frameworks, it demonstrates enhancement of a ViT-based backbone, not a direct original-ViT-versus-CNN controlled ranking. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:f3405d317606]

Efficiency comparisons likewise depend on which model and resource metric are held fixed. HVT reports that, at comparable FLOPs, progressive token pooling makes its hierarchical visual transformer outperform competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100; its mechanism shortens the patch sequence analogously to CNN downsampling and finds average-pooled tokens more discriminative than a single class token in its experiments. LeViT reports a speed–accuracy result for a hybrid fast classifier: at 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy it is five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. These results support hierarchy, pooling and hybrid design as ways to improve efficiency, but HVT is not original ViT and LeViT is not a pure CNN; moreover, CPU speed is a hardware measurement and cannot be inferred merely from FLOPs or parameter counts. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:3e86efa21051]

The broad Battle of the Backbones evaluation is the widest modern comparison but has a different population from the original ViT experiment. Across more than 1,500 training runs spanning classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other tasks, its summary reports that supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-supervised SwinV2-Base and CLIP ViT-Base were top overall models; at smaller scales, ConvNeXt-Tiny and SwinV2-Tiny were winners, followed by DINO ViT-Small. It also states that supervised convolutional networks outperformed transformers on most tasks considered, while warning that pretraining dataset size is a confound: in apples-to-apples comparisons with matched architecture scale and similarly sized pretraining datasets, self-supervised backbones were highly competitive or outperformed supervised counterparts. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] That benchmark also reports a family-level learning-curve observation: ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and to the number of parameters. This is consistent with the original ViT paper's conditional success under large-scale pretraining and with CvT's description of ViT lagging similarly sized CNNs on smaller data. It should not be generalized to every transformer because the BoB suite includes modern ViTs, hierarchical Swin models, CLIP and self-supervised models, whereas original ViT is a non-hierarchical pure patch transformer. The experimentally defensible summary is that CNN backbones are strong and convenient under many established settings, original ViT can match or exceed convolutional networks when its large-data transfer conditions are met, and adapted or hybrid transformers are needed for some efficiency and dense-prediction interfaces. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is that the original Vision Transformer's strongest claim cannot be converted into a data-independent backbone ranking. Dosovitskiy et al. showed that a pure transformer over image patches could perform very well after large-scale pretraining and transfer, but CvT's authors describe ViT as remaining below similarly sized CNN counterparts such as ResNets when trained on smaller datasets. Battle of the Backbones later reports that ViTs are more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. The practical implication is that comparisons must state corpus size, transfer target, model size, and whether training is supervised or self-supervised; otherwise a large-data ViT result and a small-data CNN result answer different questions. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea]

A second unresolved issue is how to compare backbones fairly when pretraining recipes differ. Battle of the Backbones found supervised convolutional networks strongest on most tasks in its broad suite, but also observed that the supervised models often benefited from larger pretraining datasets; when architecture and dataset scale were matched, self-supervised backbones were highly competitive or better. Thus, architecture family, pretraining objective, and data scale are entangled. The available evidence does not justify attributing every CNN or ViT advantage solely to convolution or self-attention, and the original ViT-versus-CNN question remains conditional unless those variables are controlled. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

Dense prediction exposes a concrete task-interface limitation of original ViT. Its columnar, coarse patch tokens produce a single-scale, low-resolution representation, while detection and segmentation commonly need high-resolution, multi-stage feature maps; PVT also notes that global attention becomes computationally and memory expensive at image sizes around an 800-pixel short edge. CNN backbones already provide progressively downsampled feature maps, but that convenience is not the same as proving better classification accuracy. The open problem is to obtain global context, dense spatial detail, and multiscale outputs without paying the full cost of long token sequences or redesigning the original ViT interface. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012]

Later systems show plausible fixes, but they also change the object being evaluated. PVT adds 4×4 patches, a progressive shrinking pyramid, and spatial-reduction attention; CvT adds convolutional token embedding, hierarchical stages, and convolutional projections; ViT-CoMer adds a convolutional multi-receptive-field pyramid and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion. These designs address hierarchy, locality, or token cost, yet their results cannot be assigned to the original pure ViT. A remaining evaluation problem is therefore to disentangle gains from the attention mechanism itself from gains introduced by CNN-style pyramids, convolutions, new tokenization, or the ability to reuse particular pretrained weights. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0]

The efficiency question is also not settled by one scalar metric. Original global self-attention mixes all patch tokens, so finer patches and higher resolutions rapidly increase sequence-related compute and memory; HVT and PVT respond by pooling or spatially reducing tokens, while LeViT adopts decreasing activation-map resolutions in a hybrid fast classifier. However, parameters, FLOPs, CPU latency, GPU latency, peak memory, and token count measure different constraints. LeViT's reported five-fold CPU speed advantage over EfficientNet at 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy is hardware- and model-specific, and it cannot be generalized into a universal transformer-versus-CNN efficiency conclusion from FLOPs alone. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:3e86efa21051]

High-resolution multimodal use intensifies the token-budget problem rather than resolving the backbone comparison. ConvLLaVA replaces ViT with a hierarchical ConvNeXt encoder because redundant visual tokens create substantial compute in high-resolution large multimodal models; after high-resolution adaptation and an added compression stage, it supports 1536×1536 inputs with 576 visual tokens. This demonstrates a strong task-specific reason to favor hierarchical convolutional compression, but it is not an ImageNet-controlled comparison with original ViT. The open problem is to compare visual encoders under the same multimodal decoder, resolution, token budget, accuracy target, and hardware budget rather than inferring universal superiority from token reduction. [E:arxiv:2405.15738:abstract:claim:8b6f0b7a6a17]

Representation research raises another open problem: similar task accuracy can hide different internal strategies. CKA analyses find that ViTs maintain more uniform representations across layers, whereas ResNets separate more clearly into lower and higher stages; the study links early global information aggregation to self-attention and strong lower-to-upper feature propagation to ViT residual connections. These differences may affect robustness, localization, fine-tuning, and interpretability, but CKA similarity alone does not establish which representation is preferable. More controlled work is needed to connect architectural mechanism and representation geometry to out-of-distribution behavior, spatial localization, and transfer performance. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:ea90270388d2] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:02ab8c9650c5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:52af6f3b7abb] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31]

The conceptual boundary between Transformers and ConvNets also remains open. A unified framework interprets vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions and uses that view to replace softmax with ReLU plus Layer Normalization and to design a depth-wise vision Transformer with comparable performance and greater efficiency in its experiments. Such unification helps compare kernel banks, dynamic weights, depth-wise operations, and activation choices, but it does not show that original ViT and a static CNN backbone have identical inductive biases or deployment costs. Researchers still need evidence about which shared design components cause convergence, accuracy, or efficiency changes. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:733cf6749238] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:d87b9e51465a] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:section:abstract:3:0c1521ca20ba:claim:683bed3275bc]

Finally, hybrid and modernized backbones complicate reproducibility for practitioners. ViT-CoMer preserves a plain ViT branch so it can load open-source ViT pretraining while newly added convolutional components use different initialization; CvT removes the need for conventional positional encoding in its convolutional design; and broad benchmarks include ConvNeXt, ResNet, SwinV2, CLIP ViT, self-supervised models, and diffusion-derived encoders. This diversity means a backbone chosen for one regime may not be best for another. The concrete limitation is not a lack of models, but the difficulty of making an informed choice without matched data, task, resolution, token budget, latency, pretraining, and downstream-head conditions. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

Overall, the evidence supports a trade-off rather than a final winner. Original ViT removes convolution and gains early global mixing and a generic sequence architecture, with its best evidence under large-scale pretraining; convolutional neural-network backbones retain local weight sharing, built-in hierarchy, and dense-feature interfaces that can help under smaller-data, efficiency, or dense-prediction constraints. Adapted and hybrid models improve specific weaknesses, but each modification narrows the claim. The central open problem is therefore not whether one family is universally better, but how to isolate and match the conditions under which global attention, convolutional locality, hierarchy, token compression, and pretraining actually determine performance. ## Conclusion

The answer to the comparison is that original ViT and convolutional neural-network backbones make different architectural trades. ViT removes convolutional locality and processes image patches as a global token sequence; this supports its strongest large-data transfer results but increases attention cost as token count grows and leaves a coarse classification-oriented representation. CNN backbones encode local weight sharing and stage-wise hierarchy, making them natural feature extractors for smaller-data learning and dense-prediction frameworks, without proving universal accuracy superiority. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:620dfb14bc2b] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:757b5d61cf31] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636]

Experimental claims must remain matched to their conditions. The original ViT result supports viability under large-scale pretraining and transfer; CvT's small-data statement and Battle of the Backbones' finding that ViTs are more sensitive to pretraining-data amount and parameter count qualify rather than overturn it. PVT's COCO gains over ResNet50 or ResNeXt101, CvT's 87.7% ImageNet-1k result, and ViT-CoMer's COCO/ADE20K scores belong to adapted or hybrid systems, not to unmodified ViT. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:1535207f82c0] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:1:69b97a4ae44d:claim:9ed6923b9b67] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:2:9088148f1c89:claim:c039806fc50a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:5c79a9124ffd] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:6166499fba60] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:4:8ad541081adb:claim:138057ae0012] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:219eea121636] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:a671140fcb49] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:6dba2df4d842] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:eff216ec4dfd] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:f7bb41f9fce0] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:f3405d317606] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:94f8fb4049ea] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:30495836476d]

Thus there is no defensible family-independent winner. CNN backbones are convenient when local priors, hierarchical maps, constrained pretraining or dense tasks dominate; original ViT is compelling when large corpora support learning visual structure and early global context is valuable. Later pyramidal, token-reduced and convolutional-transformer designs address specific weaknesses, but each modification narrows the claim and requires matched data, task, resolution, token budget, latency, pretraining and head conditions.
